title: Probability
description: Animated KS3 Maths lesson on probability for ages 9 to 14: probability words and the probability scale from 0 to 1, working out probabilities as fractions, the probability of something not happening, expected results, and listing outcomes for two events.
intro: How likely is it? Probability words, the 0 to 1 scale, fractions, expected results and two events, explained by the owl in five short parts.

steps.say: **Probability** tells us how likely something is to happen. We can use words: impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely and certain.
Rolling a 7 on a dice numbered 1 to 6 is **impossible**. Getting heads when you flip a fair coin is an **even chance**. The Sun rising tomorrow is **certain**.
We can also use numbers. Impossible is **0**. Certain is **1**. An even chance is {1/2}, or 0.5. Every probability is somewhere from 0 to 1.
steps.speak: We can also use numbers. Impossible is 0. Certain is 1. An even chance is one half, or 0.5. Every probability is somewhere from 0 to 1.

check.q: A drawer has only red socks in it. You take one sock without looking. How likely is it to be red?
check.hint: Is there any other colour it could be?
check.explain: Every sock is red, so it **must** be red: it is **certain**, with a probability of 1.

steps.say: When all the outcomes are equally likely: **probability = number of ways it can happen ÷ total number of outcomes**.
steps.speak: When all the outcomes are equally likely, the probability is the number of ways it can happen, divided by the total number of outcomes.

steps.say: A fair dice has 6 equally likely outcomes. There is only one 6, so the probability of rolling a 6 is {1/6}.
steps.speak: A fair dice has 6 equally likely outcomes. There is only one 6, so the probability of rolling a 6 is one sixth.

steps.say: Rolling a number greater than 4 can happen 2 ways: a 5 or a 6. So the probability is {2/6}, which simplifies to {1/3}.
steps.speak: Rolling a number greater than 4 can happen 2 ways: a 5 or a 6. So the probability is two sixths, which simplifies to one third.

steps.say: A bag has 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green counters. That is 10 counters. 5 are blue, so the probability of picking blue is {5/10} = {1/2}.
steps.speak: A bag has 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green counters. That is 10 counters. 5 are blue, so the probability of picking blue is five tenths, which equals one half.

check.q: A bag has 4 red and 6 yellow counters. One is taken at random. What is the probability that it is red?
check.hint: First count all the counters. How many of them are red?
check.explain: There are 4 + 6 = 10 counters and 4 are red, so the probability is {4/10} = **{2/5}**.

steps.say: Something either happens or it doesn't. The two probabilities always **add up to 1**.
The probability of rain tomorrow is 0.3. So the probability of **no rain** is 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.
steps.speak: The probability of rain tomorrow is 0.3. So the probability of no rain is 1 minus 0.3, which is 0.7.

steps.say: Back to the bag of 10 counters. The probability of green is {2/10}. So the probability of **not green** is 1 − {2/10} = {8/10} = {4/5}.
steps.speak: Back to the bag of 10 counters. The probability of green is two tenths. So the probability of not green is 1 minus two tenths, which is eight tenths, or four fifths.

check.q: The probability that a team wins its next match is 0.6. What is the probability that it does not win?
check.hint: Winning and not winning add up to 1.

steps.say: If you repeat something many times, you can work out how many times you **expect** an outcome: **probability × number of tries**.
steps.speak: If you repeat something many times, you can work out how many times you expect an outcome: probability times number of tries.

steps.say: Flip a fair coin 200 times. The probability of heads is {1/2}, and {1/2} × 200 = 100. So we expect about 100 heads.
steps.speak: Flip a fair coin 200 times. The probability of heads is one half, and one half times 200 equals 100. So we expect about 100 heads.

steps.say: This spinner has 4 equal parts and 1 is red. Spin it 80 times: {1/4} × 80 = 20. We expect red about 20 times.
steps.speak: This spinner has 4 equal parts and 1 is red. Spin it 80 times: one quarter times 80 equals 20. We expect red about 20 times.

steps.say: Real results are usually close, but not exact. And a coin has **no memory**: after 5 heads in a row, the chance of heads next time is still {1/2}.
steps.speak: Real results are usually close, but not exact. And a coin has no memory: after 5 heads in a row, the chance of heads next time is still one half.

check.q: A fair dice numbered 1 to 6 is rolled 60 times. About how many times would you expect to roll a 6?
check.hint: The probability of a 6 is {1/6}. What is {1/6} of 60?

steps.say: Flip two coins. List every outcome carefully: HH, HT, TH and TT. That is 4 equally likely outcomes.
Only one of the 4 outcomes is two heads, so the probability of two heads is {1/4}.
steps.speak: Only one of the 4 outcomes is two heads, so the probability of two heads is one quarter.

steps.say: Now flip a coin **and** roll a dice. A table helps you list every outcome without missing any.
The coin has 2 outcomes and the dice has 6, so there are 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes. The probability of heads and a 6 is {1/12}.
steps.speak: The coin has 2 outcomes and the dice has 6, so there are 2 times 6, which is 12 outcomes. The probability of heads and a 6 is one twelfth.

check.q: Two fair coins are flipped. What is the probability of getting one head and one tail?
check.hint: Look at the list HH, HT, TH, TT. How many of them have one head and one tail?
check.explain: HT and TH both have one head and one tail: 2 out of 4, so the probability is {2/4} = **{1/2}**.
